Cette année, La Converse a poursuivi le: This year, La Converse continued the socially engaged rap project Les Messagers Converse, which began last year. As a reminder, the initiative gives young Montréal rappers the chance to express their concerns through their art.
Au total, cinq jeunes ont chacun posé un: In all, five young people each laid down a verse over an original production (by Birdzonthetrack, a Montréal beatmaker who supported them from start to finish), creating a one-of-a-kind song that they decided, together with La Converse, to title C'est pas la fin du hood.
Pour être tout à fait honnête, mon trava:
To be completely honest, my work on this project wasn’t only journalistic, but logistical too. I was there for every stage of the production: the auditions, the selection of the participants, the writing workshops with Raccoon, and the creation of the final project.
There were a few hiccups along the way, but I think I mostly faced two major challenges.
La première, c’est l’absence de filles d: The first is the absence of girls in this project. Unfortunately, the fact that there are five boys and no girls on the track is hard to miss. But don’t get me wrong: La Converse did everything it could to have at least one female rapper on the song, and there were some at the start. Initially, two female rappers were taking part in the project. They had to withdraw, however, because of logistical constraints and a lack of coordination. Nothing too serious.
La deuxième limite a été la nécessité de: The second limitation was the need to constantly rely on last year’s product. New young people means, in a way, a new project too. Our youth were excellent in this project, both this year and last year. Still, several times, in order to respect their integrity, I had to force myself to look at this year’s MCs with fresh eyes and stop comparing them to the others. It’s a bit like a mom comparing her youngest to her oldest; it’s not healthy for anyone!
Bref, j’ai tenté du mieux que j’ai pu de: In short, I did my best to introduce you to the MCs of 2024, who rap about the reality of their neighbourhoods and the people around them.
Bonne lecture et à bientôt !: Enjoy the read, and see you soon!
Ils ne se connaissent pas, mais lorsqu’i: They don’t know each other, but when they walk into La Converse’s studios for the first time, the chemistry between Genki, Chérubin, Versatol, SMG and YBB is instant. Knowing laughter and jokes fly between these five young men who – they don’t know it yet – are about to create something that will exceed their expectations.
Après presque deux mois de rencontres he: After nearly two months of weekly meetings and learning under the mentorship of <l1>Raccoon</l1>, they record a song in the studio as well as a music video about the different subjects they tackle in their track. Among these themes are addiction, gun violence and the hypersexualization experienced by young people in their city.
En décrivant comment ils voient ce qui l: By describing how they see the world around them, the Messagers Converse act as true journalists, informing anyone who wants to know about the reality of their neighbourhood and their community.

Nous sommes à la mi-juin, c’est le début: It’s mid-June, the start of summer. On the fourth floor of a building in the Ahuntsic neighbourhood, the Messagers Converse arrive one after another and discover the Toosik recording studios. The big day has arrived: today they’re recording their song C’est pas la fin du hood. For some, it’s a regular session; for others, it’s their first time in a studio. We met the MCs in the heat of the action.
Adam, de son nom d’artiste Genki, The De: Adam, whose artist name is Genki, The Developer, a rapper from Saint-Léonard. Photo: Amélie Rock
Quand Genki, The Developer se met à rapp: When Genki, The Developer starts rapping, it’s easy to find the Montréal soul in his verses. Whether in his choice of words or the slang he uses, the young rapper from Saint-Léonard is well aware of the reality around him and his people.
À peine âgé de 20 ans, il s’est lancé da: Barely 20 years old, he got into music a year and a half ago. Of Algerian and Spanish descent, Adam is a neighbourhood kid who isn’t afraid to say so. “I’m from Saint-Léonard,” he says right off the bat. “For me, my neighbourhood is like a second home. It’s a familiar place for me, I grew up there,” he says.
Conscient de la réalité des jeunes racis: Aware of the reality facing racialized youth in Saint-Léonard like himself, he says music came along and, in a way, saved him from the problems of the street, which affect more and more isolated young people. “When I started music, I saw rap as a kind of story to tell through words. It was a synonym for hope for me,” he explains.
« Avec le rap, tu peux créer un lien ave: “With rap, you can create a connection with everyone who’s listening to you. You can use your lived experience, and with that, you can touch and inspire a lot of people,” he thinks. One of the reasons he feels so connected to music is that, thanks to it, he finds it easier to express his reality and his emotions.
« À la fin, on est tous des humains, con: “In the end, we’re all human,” Genki concludes. “What matters when you’re young, especially when you come from a hood, is knowing what’s good and what’s bad. You have to be able to tell the negative choices from the positive ones, and the impact they can have on us and on others.” The message he wants to pass on to his peers comes through clearly in his verse on the Messagers Converse song. “There’s so much more in your hood; get up and get moving!” he raps.
Justin, alias BigJ Chérubin, a commencé: Justin, aka BigJ Chérubin, started rapping a few months ago. Photo: Amélie Rock
Il y a quelques mois à peine, Justin a c: Just a few months ago, Justin started using the mic to express himself. Rather shy and introverted by nature, he loves to write. “I love music for the creative side, because you can put images in people’s heads,” he confides.
Né d’une mère haïtienne et d’un père qué: Born to a Haitian mother and a Québécois father, BigJ Chérubin grew up on the outskirts of Montréal. He feels rap came along at a perfect moment in his life: “It let me say out loud what I was thinking quietly. I was closed off for a long time, and now I use rap to get out what I had bottled up, what I saw and lived through when I was younger,” he explains in one breath.
Pour lui, le rap est tout un art, et est: For him, rap is a whole art form, and a very technical one. “When we grow up, muscles develop in the body, but also in the voice. Words form in the heart, then in the head,” he says passionately. Those words eventually come out and finally reach other people, and for Justin, that’s what rap is.
« Il y a beaucoup de jeunes qui se cherc: “There are a lot of young people who are searching for themselves, who don’t necessarily have confidence in themselves and in what they can accomplish. Unfortunately, some of them will gain that confidence in the wrong place,” Justin explains. He adds that he sees a lot of himself in Montréal’s youth today. “I didn’t have confidence in myself, but the older you get, the more choices open up to you. I think younger people have to see life as a marathon. It’s long, but it’s not hard; you just have to keep going and not give up,” he reflects.
Apprendre de ses erreurs et bâtir sur ce: Learning from your mistakes and building on those lessons would be the ultimate advice Chérubin would give to anyone looking for some. He feels he has been “lucky” because, in a way, music came along and saved him. In his verse on C’est pas la fin du hood, he talks a lot about how easy it is to get lost in life when you’re young. “Everything happens fast, but you can’t rush. You have to find the time to blossom!”
Versatol – Mistral, pour les intimes – e: Versatol – Mistral to those close to him – is from Fabreville, in Laval. Photo: Amélie Rock
Le vécu de Mistral, un jeune homme dans: The life Mistral has lived, as a young man in his twenties, has been heavy. He was born to Haitian parents and grew up in the Fabreville neighbourhood of Laval. He’s proud of it, too, and doesn’t hesitate to mention it when you talk with him.
« La musique et l’écriture ont toujours: “Music and writing have always been part of my life,” Versatol tells us. It was first the creative side of writing that won him over. “I started writing a lot in elementary school. I wrote down everything I saw, what I felt, what I lived through. Then it turned into little stories, into poems, and as I got older it became slam and rap,” he recounts.
Versatol nous confie que, lorsqu’il étai: Versatol confides that, when he was younger, he had a hard time getting through certain ordeals. “I got picked on a lot, for who I was, how I talked, what I looked like. It affected me a lot,” he says. He adds, however, that it’s in a way thanks to that that he took refuge in music. “I spent a lot of time alone, and that let me explore music in depth.”
Versatol a choisi de parler des problème: Versatol chose to talk about drug use problems and how they affect his neighbourhood, but also every hood in the city and their youth. His reality, like that of many others, was “absent parents and a void that had to be filled,” he writes in C'est pas la fin du hood.
« Garder ça et rester <em>clean </em>»,: “Hold on to that and stay clean,” even if it’s hard, is the message Versatol has for everyone facing the world of the street. He ends the Messagers Converse song with a message of hope, in which he says that “behind it all, the hood is hurting; behind it all, with a pen and paper, we can express our passion.”

C’est en rigolant avec son groupe d’amis: It was while joking around with his group of friends in high school that SMG (Samuel, by his first name) first tried rap. He had no idea then that those laughs among friends would take him so much further.
SMG a grandi seul avec son grand-père su: SMG grew up alone with his grandfather on the South Shore. His parents weren’t able to raise him, he tells us openly. “My mother had an accident very young, and my father was caught up in street-related problems,” he explains.
Très jeune, il devient un « mauvais garç: Very young, he became a “bad boy,” in his words. “Trouble with the law, lots of school changes, and so on,” he lists. “I often had to make new friends, which meant I ended up alone a bunch of times.” He says, however, that when he started rapping, he got a lot of support from the people around him.
« Il y a quelques mois, l’un de mes amis: “A few months ago, one of my friends died. It shook us all,” he says of his friends. “He was someone who backed me all the way in rap, but also in everything in general.” He lived his successes and good times with him. Everything was shared. “That was taken from me, it’s something I can’t live with him anymore,” he says sadly.
Son ami a tragiquement perdu la vie dans: His friend tragically lost his life in circumstances linked to gun violence. He wants to send an important message to the youth of his city, but also to those whose mandate is to protect them. “I realized anyone can get killed for nothing. Good people who don’t deserve to die lose their lives in the snap of a finger. But we’re in reality, and we have to learn the lessons from it; that’s what I’m trying to do with my music,” he explains.
« Laisser tomber l’environnement dangere: “Leave behind the dangerous environment of the street and focus on your dreams”: those are SMG’s wise words. Being able to live is a privilege, he believes. “If you have a life, you have to have a dream and do everything to make it happen. Don’t wait until it’s too late to regret it – whether it’s prison or death,” he finishes in a firm tone.

Originaire du Bangladesh, YBB Wit Da Hea: Originally from Bangladesh, YBB Wit Da Heat (YBB to those close to him) is a devoted lover of rap. The years he spent growing up in the Ahuntsic neighbourhood, in the north of the city, shaped his personality and gave him an honest view of the reality of the street in the metropolis.
« Je fais de la musique depuis l’époque: “I’ve been making music since the pandemic,” he says right away. Plus jeune, YBB ne voyait pas souvent so: When he was younger, YBB didn’t see his father often. “He worked a lot, I only saw him one day a week. Seeing how much he sacrificed for his family, especially for his kids, motivated me a lot to work just as hard once I got older,” he says.
Le jeune homme de 19 ans a passé une gra: The 19-year-old spent much of his youth with his older brothers. “I hung out a lot with people older than me, they taught me a lot of things, good and bad…” he says. Ahnaf feels that by spending time with “the OGs of the hood,” he matured faster than other young people his age.
L’une des problématiques dont YBB parle: One of the issues YBB talks about in his songs is the gap between his parents’ generation and his own, especially in immigrant families. “I see a lot of young people my age lying to their parents, taking advantage of the fact that they don’t speak the language well or don’t know how the system here works… I think it’s an opportunity for us to build bonds with others and we’re throwing it away,” he explains.
Pour lui, tout ça est lié à la question: For him, all of this is tied to the question of identity, which is very blurry for many young Montrealers from immigrant backgrounds. “I try to show how some people try to project a false image of themselves, and what the consequences of that are for younger people,” he says, speaking of the problems he sees around him.
Ahnaf pense que le plus important chez l: Ahnaf thinks that what matters most among young people is influence. “You can’t let yourself be influenced, you have to be inspired by what you see instead,” he finally says. Young people’s judgment is shaped by what they see and hear, and that’s why YBB decided to speak up and rap on C’est pas la fin du hood.
<strong>Exprimer la réalité du <em>hood<: Expressing the reality of the hood through song
Violence armée, mauvaise influence, cons: Gun violence, bad influences, drug use… Reading the broad strokes, it’s easy to fall into a stigmatized view of the hood and what it represents. But for our five MCs, C'est pas la fin du hood is an anthem of hope. It’s a promise of success for young people from neighbourhoods that tend to be forgotten or, worse, judged negatively.
Ainsi, Genki, The Developer, BigJ Chérub: Genki, The Developer, BigJ Chérubin, Versatol, SMG and YBB Wit Da Heat are young rappers engaged in their community, but also valuable members of their neighbourhoods and of the city. Through their ability to use the art of rap and music to describe the main concerns that torment their people, they are true ambassadors of the hood.
